turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Mrs Pell's here, doctor, and her husband's come in with her. Blood pressure was one thirty-two over eighty-four, pulse sixty-eight, and seventy-eight kilos on our scales. I can hold a blood-room slot straight after if you end up wanting bloods.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Give me a moment, the screen's frozen solid. Right. Mrs Pell, what's been going on?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, I've been tired all the time. I don't know, doctor. Work's flat out, and I'm fifty-three, so I figured it was just the job and getting older.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long have you felt this tired?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Months. I can't pin down when it started. I really don't know.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was March, love. A good five months. She nods off on the couch every arvo, doctor, I've watched her.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Not every arvo. Some days, I'll admit. And I don't know that it was March — could've been later. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that bit again? The computer just beeped at me. You're not sure it was March?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): No. He says March. All I can tell you is months. I don't know any better than that.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you been feeling the cold?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Heaps. I'll have a jumper on and the heater going and I'm still cold, hands especially. Been about as long as the tiredness.

[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She'll sit there with a blanket over her knees. And she's hardly eating, which is the weird part, because she's gone from seventy-one kilos up to that seventy-eight.

[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): The weight, yes. I'm not hardly eating, though. I take the same lunch to work I always have, and if anything there's a bit more toast at night. I don't know where he's got that from.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): OK. So the weight's come up. Was that sudden, or gradual?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Gradual. I don't know, alongside the tiredness, I suppose. Not like, in a week. I did just blame my age.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your bowels — any constipation?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No, that's all fine. I go regularly.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's the mood been?
[SEG0019] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Flat as anything. She won't see anyone on the weekends. Hasn't been herself for months, whatever she tells you.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm a bit flat, I'll say that, but it's the work. I'm not avoiding people — we went to my sister's on Sunday. I wouldn't call it depression. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, can you do the mood part again? I was clicked into the wrong window.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit down when work piles up. I still get everything done. It doesn't feel like a proper illness to me.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Earlier you said the bowels were fine. Any hard stools, or straining?

[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, actually... yeah. I was wrong before. I've been blocked up the last few weeks. Every second day, or third, and it's hard. I don't know why I told you it was normal.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood when you go, or pain in the tummy?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No blood. No pain. Just slow, that's all.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, she's been buying those prune packs for ages. I'd call it a couple of months, not a few weeks.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll note you two don't agree on the timing. Any thyroid problems in the family?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Mum. Underactive thyroid, she was on thyroxine most of her life. Dad's fine, I think. I don't know the ins and outs.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): And have you had your own thyroid checked?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Years ago. They said borderline. I don't know, doctor — maybe six years back, could be longer. I never chased it up.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me get the old path up. Sorry, it's spinning again. Here — TSH back then was 2.1, that's normal, not borderline, and the free T4 was normal too.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh. Well, maybe that was the cholesterol they called borderline. I muddle the two. I don't know.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Happens. Are you taking anything regular, scripts or from the chemist?

[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Vitamin D, a thousand units, most mornings. I forget it, maybe twice a week. I also had magnesium for a fortnight and then I stopped, about a month ago. My sister swears by it for cramps. I never actually got cramps.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Vitamin D dose once more? That line didn't stick.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): A thousand units. Most mornings. I miss about two a week. I don't know if that's a problem.

[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Putting the cold, the tiredness, the weight and the constipation with your mum's history, this could be an underactive thyroid. Could also just be the workload and age. I can't say which yet.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. If that's what you reckon. I still think it's work, though.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. We'll get bloods — TSH, free T4, and a full blood count. You don't need to fast.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight either way and we'll look at them together. Keep the vitamin D going as you have been. If the TSH is up we'll talk about thyroxine then — nothing to start today.
[SEG0042] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll walk her round now, doctor. The blood-room slot's still held.

features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Constipation includes hard stools/straining; patient said bowel motions are every second or third day and hard after initially denying constipation.
Negative finding: patient initially denied constipation/bowel problems ('No... that's all fine. I go regularly') before correcting herself later.
Prior thyroid tests were described by the doctor as normal: TSH 2.1 and free T4 normal, contradicting the patient's recollection that they were 'borderline'.
Patient clarified that what had been called 'borderline' may have been cholesterol, not thyroid tests.
Plan includes that no thyroxine is to be started today.
